title: The Lost Colony
bigUnderstanding: Historians reason from evidence, like scientists, and some questions are still open. A strong answer is the one the evidence best supports, stated with the right confidence. Also plants seeds for Jamestown: supply ships, relationships with Native nations, and drought.

opening.intro: In 1587, 115 English men, women and children landed on an island off North Carolina. Three years later, every single one of them was gone. Nobody has proven what happened. Yet.

video.title: How Roanoke Vanished Into Thin Air

cards.label: Your job
cards.text: Figure out what most likely happened to 115 people. You win by making a strong case for your answer, using the evidence. Nobody has the official answer.

cards.label: Why England was here
cards.text: Spain was getting rich from its American colonies. Queen Elizabeth wanted England in the game, so she let Sir Walter Raleigh try to start England's first colony.

cards.label: Try #1 (1585)
cards.text: About 100 soldiers built a fort on Roanoke Island. They ran short of food, fought with the local tribes, and went home a year later.

cards.label: Try #2 (1587)
cards.text: This time: families. Their governor was John White, an artist. They planned to settle farther north, but the ship's pilot dropped them back at Roanoke.

cards.label: Who already lived here
cards.text: Algonquian-speaking nations, like the Roanoke, Secotan and Croatoan peoples. They'd lived on this coast for centuries.

cards.label: 1590: White returns
cards.text: White sailed home for supplies and got stuck in England for three years. When he finally came back, he saw smoke on the island. He fired a cannon. No answer.

opening.prompt: What do you want to look at first?

facilitatorNotes: Abi has seen the context cards (Raleigh, the 1585 fort, the 1587 families, the Native nations, White's 1590 return) and may have watched a 2-minute Smithsonian Channel video about the mystery. Don't re-explain that background unless she asks.

This mystery is genuinely unsolved. NEVER tell Abi a theory is wrong or 'not correct.' For any theory, say which clues support it and which are a problem for it, and let her weigh them. A theory with strong evidence against it (like 'lost at sea') can still be argued if she handles that evidence honestly.
Give Abi the evidence as an investigator would find it: White's 1590 observations, earlier records, later reports, archaeology, and tree rings.
Tree rings are a great science hook: if she asks how rings show rainfall, explain briefly (wide rings = good growing years, narrow = drought).

Treat Native nations as real people with their own interests, not props. Croatoan (Manteo's people) were allies; relations with the Secotan and Roanoke people had turned violent during the earlier 1585–86 expedition.
If she asks about Jamestown, she can learn that Jamestown was settled in 1607, 17 years later, about 130 miles north. Don't push it.
Pin real events to her timeline as they come up (1587 colony arrives; Aug 18, 1587 Virginia Dare born; 1588 Spanish Armada; Aug 1590 White returns).
justInTimeConcepts: Primary vs. secondhand sources (White saw the carvings himself; Strachey heard a claim years later).
Tree rings as a record of rainfall.
Archaeology: objects can travel by trade, so a find doesn't prove who carried it.
scaffolds: What did the colonists leave behind on purpose, and what does that tell you?
Which evidence was seen firsthand, and which was reported by someone later?
Is there one explanation, or could the group have split up?
completion: Abi has examined at least 3 pieces of evidence and made her case: her verdict, 2–3 supporting clues, one clue that doesn't fit and how she explains it, and her confidence. Any evidence-backed verdict wins.

endReveal.concept: Historical reasoning: weighing primary and secondhand sources, and stating conclusions with honest confidence when a question is unresolved.

vocabulary.meaning: Evidence from someone who was there.
When separate pieces of evidence back each other up.
Dating events and climate using tree rings.

realVsConstructed.real: Everything in this case: the colony, John White, Virginia Dare, the carvings, the war with Spain, the drought shown by tree rings, and the later reports and digs.
realVsConstructed.constructed: Nothing invented. The mystery is still open today.

data.question: What most likely happened to the Roanoke colonists between 1587 and 1590?
data.trueExplanation: NOT AN ANSWER KEY. Historians lean toward an orderly departure (houses taken down, CROATOAN carved, no distress cross), likely to Croatoan and/or inland, with drought making survival harder. But the question is open. Any theory Abi backs with evidence, while honestly facing the evidence against it, can win.
causalChain: War with Spain delays him 3 years
Colonists leave in an orderly way

evidence.label: Who the colonists were
evidence.result: About 115 people, including families: men, women and children. White's daughter Eleanor Dare gave birth to Virginia Dare on August 18, 1587, the first English child born in the Americas.

evidence.label: Why John White left
evidence.result: Late summer 1587 the colonists were short of supplies. They begged their governor, White, to sail to England and bring more. He left about nine days after his granddaughter was born.

evidence.label: Why it took three years to return
evidence.result: England was at war with Spain. In 1588 the Queen kept ships home to fight the Spanish Armada. White's small 1588 attempt was attacked at sea and robbed. He only got back in August 1590.

evidence.label: The carvings
evidence.result: "CROATOAN" carved in capital letters on a post at the fort entrance. "CRO" carved on a tree near the shore.

evidence.label: What the colonists agreed with White before he left
evidence.result: If they moved, they'd carve where they went. If they left in distress or danger, they'd carve a cross above it. White found NO cross.

evidence.label: The settlement and fort
evidence.result: The houses had been taken down. A strong palisade (wall of tall tree trunks) had been built. Heavy iron items and lead were left lying in the grass, overgrown.

evidence.label: White's buried chests
evidence.result: White had buried his own chests. They'd been dug up and broken open. His books were torn, his maps and pictures rotted by rain, his armor rusted.

evidence.label: Who lived on Croatoan
evidence.result: Croatoan (today's Hatteras Island) was about 50 miles south. It was home to Manteo's people. Manteo had traveled to England and was an ally of the English.

evidence.label: How things were with other Native neighbors
evidence.result: An earlier English expedition (1585–86) had violent conflict with the nearby Secotan and Roanoke people, including killing their leader Wingina. In July 1587 a colonist, George Howe, was killed by warriors while fishing alone.

evidence.label: Why White didn't go to Croatoan
evidence.result: Storms hit. Seven sailors drowned landing a boat. Anchors were lost. The captains refused to continue, and they sailed away. White never saw his family again.

evidence.label: Tree-ring data from that region
evidence.result: Ancient bald cypress trees near the Virginia–North Carolina border show 1587–1589 was the driest three-year stretch in 800 years. Crops would have failed, for colonists and Native people alike.

evidence.label: Later reports from Jamestown
evidence.result: Around 1612, Jamestown writer William Strachey reported hearing that Powhatan had killed English people living among another tribe to the north. He wasn't there; it's a secondhand report from decades later.

evidence.label: Archaeology on Hatteras Island
evidence.result: Digs have found some English objects from around that time mixed into a Native village site. Archaeologists debate whether colonists brought them or they arrived by trade.

evidence.label: John White's map
evidence.result: In 2012, researchers found a hidden symbol under a patch on White's own map, marking a spot inland near Albemarle Sound. Digs nearby found some English-style pottery. Still debated.

evidence.label: The smoke White saw
evidence.result: The smoke turned out to come from fires in the grass and woods, not a camp. No people were found.

theories.theory: They moved to Croatoan and lived with Manteo's people
They starved or died of sickness
They split up: some to Croatoan, some inland
They tried to sail home and were lost at sea

redHerrings: The dug-up chests (likely dug up after the colonists left)
